name: Mestanolone

lead: Mestanolone is a mid-20th-century oral steroid derived from DHT. It was sold as a medicine but turned out to be mostly androgenic rather than strongly anabolic.
It is largely discontinued, and the literature on it is mostly about detecting it in doping control.

paras: It activates the androgen receptor directly and cannot convert to estrogen. The 17-methyl group allows oral activity.
Reported effects include virilisation and liver damage. It is Schedule III in the US and controlled in many other countries.

lead: Mestanolone (methylandrostanolone, 17α-methyldihydrotestosterone) is a synthetic androgen and anabolic steroid, a 17α-methylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone (DHT). The methyl group makes it active by mouth, unlike DHT itself.[1]

It was first synthesised in 1935, developed by Roussel in the 1950s and marketed by about 1960, for example as 25 mg sublingual tablets (Ermalone). It was later found to be mainly androgenic with weak anabolic effects. It remains available in Japan but is mostly discontinued elsewhere.[1]

It cannot be aromatised to estrogen. Like other 17α-alkylated steroids it is reported to be hepatotoxic, and virilisation is a listed side effect.[1] It is also a metabolite of oxymetholone and has been studied mostly in doping analysis.[2]
infobox: US Schedule III; controlled in many countries[1]

paras: Mestanolone is an androgen receptor agonist with strong androgenic and weak anabolic effects, with no estrogenic or progestogenic activity.[1] Its metabolism includes epimerisation at the 17 position, studied as part of doping analysis of 17α-methyl steroids.[3][4]
Wikipedia lists virilisation (acne, hair growth, voice changes) and liver damage among its adverse effects.[1]

It was reportedly used by East German Olympic athletes in state-sponsored doping in the 1970s and 1980s.[1] Mestanolone and its metabolites are targets in anti-doping and racing-horse testing, and it has also been detected in hair.[5][6] Non-medical use is generally illicit where it is controlled.[1]
No studies found. Published papers in the sources reviewed are analytical studies on metabolism and detection.

timeline.event: Developed by Roussel; marketed by about 1960.[1]
